Before we name any fraction, I want you to notice one thing: the pieces have to be equal. If the pieces are different sizes, counting them does not give a fair fraction of the whole.
Here is one whole split into four equal pieces. Shade one piece and you can see exactly what one quarter means: one of four equal parts.
Now the whole has six equal parts. Use the picture rather than guessing from the numbers.

A fraction has two numbers, and they are doing different jobs. I want those jobs to feel obvious before we do anything more complicated.
Look at 3/8. The 3 is above the bar: it counts the parts we have selected. That is the numerator.
Your turn: focus only on the top number and what it counts.
Now look below the bar. The 8 tells us the whole is made from eight equal parts. That is the denominator.
The denominator is not 'how many are shaded'. It tells us the size and number of equal parts in one whole.
Try that role on a different fraction. Ignore whether the fraction is large or small; the positions keep their meaning.

Some fraction comparisons are much easier than they first look because the fractions already share a structure.
If the denominators match, the pieces are the same size. So five eighths beats three eighths simply because five pieces is more than three.
Use that same-denominator idea here.
When the numerators match, the question changes. Three fifths and three sevenths both have three pieces, but fifths are bigger pieces than sevenths.
That is the part students often reverse: with the same numerator, the smaller denominator gives the larger pieces.
Try a same-numerator comparison and picture the piece sizes if you need to.
So there are two clean rules: same denominator, compare how many pieces; same numerator, compare how big the pieces are.

Fractions are numbers, so every fraction has a position on a number line. The key is to count intervals, not tick marks.
From 0 to 1 is one whole. Split that distance into four equal intervals and each interval is one quarter.
Read the first marked point using those equal intervals.
A numerator tells you how many of those equal intervals to move from zero. Five eighths means five eighth-sized steps from zero.
The same idea keeps going beyond one. One whole is four quarters, so one quarter past one is five quarters from zero.
Read this point by counting equal intervals from zero.
Denominator sets the interval size; numerator counts the intervals travelled. Tick marks are only boundaries.
Now take the idea past one and keep counting the same-sized fractional intervals.
If you can see fractions as positions rather than just shaded pieces, comparison and improper fractions make much more sense.

Fractions can be written in different forms, and the form tells us something about the size of the number.
A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator, so the value is less than one whole.
Classify this one by comparing numerator and denominator.
An improper fraction has numerator at least as large as the denominator. That includes fractions equal to one, like 6/6.
A mixed number writes whole units first and then a proper fractional part, like 2 and 3/5.
Use those definitions on this boundary case.
Do not memorise the names as labels only. Connect them to size: below one, at least one, or wholes plus a fraction.
This one is written as a mixed number. Classify the form, not the size of the digits.
The next two skills will convert between improper and mixed forms, so recognising the forms cleanly comes first.
